maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. MARCOUX  PAROLE GRANTED LEOPOLD DION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
Even though this matter does not concern me personally, I presume that the house will give me its unanimous consent.
Over the week end my residence was deluged with visitors and phone calls concerning the case of Leopold Dion who was found guilty of the murder of four children.
Last week, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) promised me to appoint a lawyer and a psychiatrist to look into Dion's record.
I am not raising this matter now since it is sub judice, but I am referring rather to the evidence taken following those tragedies. Dion himself stated that he had corrupted 21 youngsters since his last parole. Will they be 21 future criminals?
Allow me to quote the opinion of Hon. Justice Lucien Cannon who had recommended life imprisonment, in Dion's case.
On June 2, 1940, he had stated, according to L'Action of July 2, 1963:
In such a case, parole should never be granted.
According to Le Soleil of July 26, 1963, Charles Edouard Cantin, assistant solicitor general of the province of Quebec, had applied for the repeal of Dion's ticket-of-leave, in order that he serve his life sentence. Even Le Devoir of this morning pointed out that Mr. Cantin had objected to Justice George Street, but he noted that the judge did not remember his former protests.
Mr. Roger Champoux wrote in La Presse of July 26, 1963:
But until the outcome, how many mysteries remain to be solved, how many concerns have to be quieted and how many questions asked will never receive a clear and definite answer.
Considering that the Profumo case has given rise to a royal inquiry in Great Britain even though there has been no loss of life, I respectfully submit that the national parole board should also be subject to a full royal inquiry.
I understand that the board is supposed to be independent but, in view of the circumstances, we need more than just a simple investigation.
Even though there are political differences between the hon. members for Quebec East, Portneuf and Saguenay and myself, I am sure that they will agree with me on that point because some of their constituents are directly affected by that tragedy.
Considering that sexual perverts are mentally sick, probably the Criminal Code should be amended so as to provide complete and adequate therapy for such people before they are eligible for parole.
As a doctor, I appreciate that psychopaths cannot be treated the same way as run-of-the-mill prisoners.
I therefore appeal to the feelings of the Minister of Justice because his children or his grandchildren could be the victims of such a tragedy just as well as ours.
Before I conclude, I should like to say that it might be appropriate to consider the resignation of Justice Street since he seems to

Question of Privilege
have made a decision without even having all the facts before him.
So I ask the Minister of Justice to order a royal inquiry regarding the national parole board.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. MARCOUX  PAROLE GRANTED LEOPOLD DION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not object to the hon. member raising that matter in the house, even though I do not believe the case at issue warrants a question of privilege.
Be that as it may, as I was entering the house, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmo-rency (Mr. Marcoux) supplied me with a copy of the statement he intended to make in this chamber to ask that a royal inquiry be made into that matter.
As I have already said, the government and the Department of Justice feel that is a most serious matter. Furthermore, and having read as the hon. member did the statements published in the week-end newspapers about it, I inquired and prepared a few notes I should like to put on record.
As I just said, I read in the week-end newspapers certain statements attributed to the assistant attorney general of the province of Quebec concerning the case of Leopold Dion. The various press reports do not establish clearly whether Mr. Charles Edouard Cantin is of the opinion, first, that his department ought to be consulted each time a request for parole is being considered and that the opinion given by his department ought to bind the national parole board or, second, that his department should be permanently represented on the board and thus share the responsibility for the decisions taken.
Besides, Mr. Cantin criticized the watch that was kept on Leopold Dion and expressed the opinion that, generally speaking, supervision should be provided by his own department.
Last Friday I informed the house that a lawyer and a psychiatrist would be asked to review that file to determine if, in this case, too great a risk was taken, in view of all the circumstances.
The policy of the former remission service and that of the present national parole board is to obtain, as soon as possible after an inmate is admitted to a penitentiary, a report from the police officers who made the investigation and one from the judge who passed the sentence. This is done to establish the

circumstances surrounding the offence and what the sentence is meant to achieve. A date of eligibility for parole is set up within six months following imprisonment, in accordance with the act and the rules. That date, according to an understanding that went into effect on January 1, 1963, is made known- and I would like the house to take note of that-to the department of the attorney general of the province of Quebec in case it should ever want to express its views about a parole that might be granted to an inmate. I am advised that since then no special communication has been received.
The department of the attorney general in a province, as Mr. Cantin said, must prosecute lawbreakers in order to protect society. I will add that it must also put at the disposal of the court, through specialized officials, information that enables the judge or the magistrate to pass the appropriate sentence. Finally it must give inmates living conditions that will facilitate their rehabilitation.
The national parole board takes into account the views, opinions and recommendations submitted by the police officers, the judge, the jailer. When it renders a decision, it has information on the offender's status before his imprisonment, it knows also the progress he has made in the penitentiary as well as his plans when he is released. It must also protect society and choose only cases that seem to warrant such a parole. If by means of preliminary consultations or a permanent representative, the department of the attorney general for the province of Quebec wishes to share the responsibility of the decisions of the board, I believe that it can be arranged easily and the board will welcome such an offer of co-operation. However, it remains to be seen if such a representative from the department of the attorney general will be able to never make a mistake. He will have, of course, to accept to be jointly responsible for the majority of decisions of the board.
I shall add only this, Mr. Speaker. Since I have already announced the appointment of a lawyer and a psychiatrist to study the case, I believe that before taking any other measures, I should wait at least for the result of that investigation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
I should like to present a report on the federal-provincial conference which took place in Ottawa last Friday and Saturday. I shall do so only briefly because, as the house is aware, the government proposes to proceed tomorrow with the legislation concerning financial assistance to municipalities which was the main subject, as it turned out, discussed at this conference. The practical results of the conference will thus be determined by parliament itself.
What the conference achieved was all that it, in itself, could achieve. That is to say, it produced what we consider to be a very satisfactory understanding with the provincial governments about the proposals that the federal government will make to this parliament. The decisions then will be in the hands of parliament.
The understanding between federal and provincial representatives can best be summarized by reading the communique which was approved at the concluding session by all members of the conference. That communique reads:
The meeting of federal and provincial governments has concluded with full agreement on the proposal of the federal government to promote employment by financial assistance, with provincial approval and co-operation to municipal capital works.
Dominion-Provincial Conference Report
The federal government indicated to the provinces that it will propose, in the legislation to be discussed in parliament next week, features which will enable the measure to be applied in forms adapted to different conditions in the various provinces.
The federal government will propose that the range of municipal works covered in the program will be broadened so as to include in any province all those municipal works which the province and the federal government believe to be productive of increased employment.
In response to suggestions from a majority of the provinces, the federal government will also propose that, if a province so wishes, it will be able to make with the proposed municipal development and loan board an agreement whereby the province is responsible for granting and administering the loans to municipalities, subject to such safeguards as are necessary to enable the board to report to parliament that expenditures have been properly made according to the purposes of the legislation.
It was agreed by all the governments that this proposed legislation can operate satisfactorily, with the agreement and co-operation of the provinces, to promote employment in Canada.
The conference also discussed the Canada pension plan recently put forward by the federal government. The discussion was conducted in the spirit of the common interest of federal and provincial governments in ensuring satisfactory provision for old age security and other welfare measures in Canada. It was agreed that further discussions between federal and provincial representatives should take place at an early date.
There was also agreement at the conference that more regular federal-provincial meetings should be held, and that it is desirable to establish more adequate machinery for maintaining federal-provincial contact between such meetings.
That, Mr. Speaker, was the agreed communique. There is just one thing I would add to the communique at this point, and that is to express in the house my warm appreciation to the eight premiers and to the representatives of the two other provinces who attended the conference. The discussions were frank, fair and friendly, and in my view were exactly what such discussions should be.
In recent years we have all had reason to become increasingly conscious of the difficulties in federal-provincial relationships. That is the reflection, fundamentally, of changing conditions, of growth and development in our country. The difficulties are not to be regretted provided that we know how to respond to the inevitable challenge which they create. The recent conference has confirmed in the fullest possible way my own faith that the challenge will be met.
The success of any form of government depends fundamentally on those it puts into positions of responsibility. In the governments of the provinces of Canada there is the spirit of co-operation, the understanding and farsightedness which Canadians need in order to improve and advance our confederation. In expressing to the provinces, as I did, my appreciation of the spirit in which they took part in the conference, I should like to

Dominion-Provincial Conference Report say above all that it will be the steady determination of this government to act in that spirit. I believe we can look forward to close and regular consultation which will be productive of the kind of co-operative federalism that will serve the aspirations of all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the objective that the Prime Minister enunciated in his concluding words there will be general agreement. He has spoken of the fine spirit of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments as evidenced by the issue of the communique to which he made reference. That is all to the good, because a matter of three or four weeks ago one would have thought that as between the government of Canada and one or two of the provinces there was not close consultation and a hot line should have been established, similar to that which was brought into being as between Khrushchev and Kennedy. However, everything is fine now according to the Prime Minister.
We are naturally pleased that consultation took place with the provinces. When this question was first before the house Her Majesty's loyal opposition asked what consultation had taken place, and there was an obvious resentment on the part of ministers of the crown to the suggestion that it should take place. We feel that consultation should be a prelude to rather than a consequence of legislation brought before parliament. I should like to add as well that what has happened has been that in almost every particular the haphazard pieces of legislation or resolutions to bring about legislation have been set aside and the demands of the provinces have been met 100 per cent.
There has been some reference to the high quality of the diplomacy exhibited by the Prime Minister at this conference.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING IN OTTAWA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
Applause is always welcome from where'er it comes. If to bargain diplomatically is to completely surrender everything for which the government of Canada stood, then this indeed was a victory for diplomacy, and provincial diplomacy at that. Having regard to the manner in which the plan of the government has been dissected, if not completely set aside, I should think "the government might very well withdraw the resolution that it has presented and introduce another one, instead of amending this resolution; because the amended resolution will bear little relationship to the original plan of the government.


We are glad to see that there has been agreement. If there had been previous consultation no doubt there would have been agreement; because the provinces, as I said a moment ago, succeeded 100 per cent in attaining their objective. What is going to happen is that the provinces will have available tremendous amounts of money from the federal government, not only for the purposes originally decided upon by the government for the projects which were referred to, but for a whole lot more projects. This was one of the suggestions we in the opposition had made, that this plan should not be restricted and further projects should be included.
Furthermore, I would add this. The plan is very much the plan we brought into effect under the winter works program. If imitation is the highest form of flattery, the high point was reached in the degree to which this plan is similar to the winter works program put in by the government of which I had the honour to be the leader. We consulted, and they agreed. We gave them control over the spending of the money, subject of course to the necessary safeguards of the federal interest. I think all of us realize that now, as a result of this conference having brought about this degree of unanimity, how much better it would have been in the interest of good feeling between federal and provincial governments if consultation had taken place in advance.
The subject of pensions was glided over by the Prime Minister with almost equal finesse to that displayed by the communique. It is very apparent that the provinces have grave doubts about the plan advanced by the federal government. That plan was introduced with a great fanfare of trumpets. It has been examined in the light of experience, and has certainly not been found to be worthy of the high commendation given to it when the resolution was introduced.
However, the provinces did not touch that. They were dealing with another large matter, the matter of securing funds to be loaned to the various municipalities. That being so, and having regard to some of the expressions of those present at the conference, I reiterate that the pension plan is going to take a long time, and full examination, to implement. I repeat what I have said on more than one occasion, that it will be months and months, if not years, before this pension plan in its entirety can be successfully launched, and the government should arrange at once for the payment of the $10 increase to the old age pensioners of Canada.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the results of the conference on

Friday and Saturday have been observed with much interest not only by those of us in the Social Credit party but by all people across the country. In the statement the Prime Minister has made he has given official confirmation to the actions which were taken. Indeed, it was the stand taken not only by myself but also by a number of other speakers on behalf of our party, when this legislation was introduced, as we were strongly in favour of the action which the government has now taken. We stressed the need that the autonomy of the provinces must be respected, and that too often the federal government disregards the position and responsibility of the provincial governments.
It is essential that we give more serious thought to this aspect of consultative government. It would have saved the government a great deal of grief with regard to the budget if just a few more people had been taken into consultation, and certainly the problems which the government has faced with respect to the municipal development and loan fund would have been eased considerably if this consultative aspect had been implemented before the legislation was introduced.
There is an interesting point here that I think important to mention. It is that a great deal can be accomplished by men of good will, even though they may have various differences, by getting together and attempting to solve their mutual problems in a spirit of harmony. The Prime Minister, the premiers and representatives of the provinces should be complimented for the progress they have made in this regard.
There are several other points in the Prime Minister's statement that are significant. He mentioned the need for more frequent provincial-federal meetings. We feel this is most important. He also mentioned the need for adequate machinery to provide for such meetings, and I would remind him that one of the suggestions we have been making for the last year or two is that there ought to be a full department of government, a ministry of provincial-federal affairs, set up to care for the problems that arise when the responsibilities of the two levels of government overlap.
I trust that the government will now give serious thought to setting up some such permanent machinery that will be adequate to take care of this very important need, a need which is growing as governments become more powerful.
With regard to the question of municipal finance I would just like to mention that the municipal development and loan fund, that has been dealt with over the week end, is only a temporary measure. It is to relieve problems of unemployment in the months
Dominion-Provincial Conference Report ahead. Unless there is some permanent machinery set up to solve the problem of municipal finance we are going to have a repetition of this situation year after year. I hope that when we return next fall the government will see fit to introduce legislation to set up a municipal development bank that would provide a source of social or public capital to take care of the public needs on a continuing basis.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition has touched on so many of the bases that are critical of the government in this matter that it does not behove me, as the representative of my party, to follow his lead, except to say that he missed working in any talk about the spirit of Hyannis Port being replaced by the spirit of Jean Lesage.
Our general feeling is that the Prime Minister's announcement is a good one. We are pleased that the unemployment measure is going to be introduced, although it is also quite apparent that in achieving this the Prime Minister and his colleagues undoubtedly gave something away. I do not know what it was they gave away, but we know they gave it away in the spirit of co-operative federalism. However, when the legislation comes before us we would like to know what it was they gave away.
So far as the pension part is concerned, I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that it was certainly slipped over in the remarks of the leader of the government. He gave us to understand, as have many other hon. members of the house, that the Canada pension plan was the cornerstone for the new Liberal government and its program and policies. Now we find that the cornerstone has not even been laid and that it is likely to be a very, very long time before it is to be set in position. That being the case, it seems to me we are justified in turning to the general promise that was made that there would be an across the board increase for old age pensioners of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $10 a month.
We will look forward to supporting the legislation this coming week or the week after, and we would be interested in knowing what changes will be made necessary in the parliamentary schedule by the fact that we can now proceed with this legislation as well as all the other pieces of legislation with which we must deal.
When the legislation is put before us we will look forward to finding out just what was the amelioration of the original proposal that led Premier Lesage and Premier Robarts in particular suddenly to become so cooperative.

3.	Are the chiefs of the staff of the (a) navy (b) army (c) air force members of this committee?
4.	In addition to Dr. Sutherland, how many civilians are members of this committee?
5.	Are all these persons civil servants?
6.	Are any members of the national research council members of this committee and, if so, how many?
7.	Are any members of the defence research board members of this committee and, if so, how many?
8.	Have any persons not normally employed by the government been hired or (contracted with) for the purpose of serving on this committee either as a member, secretary, or researcher?
9.	Is the scope of this committee limited to the review of defence spending and, if not, what are its terms of reference?
Answer: 1. There are six members of the *committee including representatives of the armed services, defence research board and the deputy minister's staff.
2.	No.
3.	No.
4.	Two.
5.	All are public servants. Employees of the defence research board are not technically civil servants, but are employed under separate regulations similar to those governing employment by the national research council.
6.	No.
7.	No. However two employees of the defence research board are included in the membership.
8.	No.
9.	The instructions given to the ad hoc committee are as described in the statement of 27 June 1963 by the Minister of National Defence to the special committee on defence:
"To assist in the review of current procurement programs and in the consideration of future policy a special advisory group has been set up in the department under the chairmanship of Dr. R. J. Sutherland, chief of operational research in the defence research board. This group has undertaken a number of studies intended to demonstrate the reasons for and against a particular course of action and to list the available options. It does not make recommendations."
The task of the ad hoc committee is essentially analytical. Advice to the Minister of National Defence on questions of defence policy remains the responsibility of senior officers and officials and, in particular, of the chiefs of staff committee.

speechtext:
1.	What is the date of the application by North Western Power Industry Limited, a subsidiary of Ventures-Frobisher Company, made to the government of Canada or any department thereof for authority to divert the waters of the Yukon river to the Taku river in Alaska?
2.	What are the conditions prescribed in the permit or other authorization to carry out the investigation or studies related thereto?
3.	What is the name of the officer of the government of Canada who recommended or issued the aforementioned permit or other authorization?
4.	On what date was the permit or other authorization terminated, and by whose order?
5.	What are the reasons for the termination of permit or other authorization?
6.	How long did the official who recommended or issued this permit or authorization remain in the employ of the government of Canada after the licence or authorization was terminated?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: * APPLICATION FOR WATER DIVERSION BY NORTH WEST POWER LTD.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like the consent of hon. members, because the reply to this question extends to some three and a half pages, to having it taken as read. Perhaps the house would consent to having it printed in Hansard.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: * APPLICATION FOR WATER DIVERSION BY NORTH WEST POWER LTD.
speechtext: Is it agreed?

maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: * APPLICATION FOR WATER DIVERSION BY NORTH WEST POWER LTD.
speechtext:
Agreed.
[Editor's note: The answer referred to above is as follows:]
1.	(a) No application was made by Northwest Power Industries Limited for authority to divert the waters of the Yukon river to the Taku river in British Columbia. Under the terms of the Dominion Water Power Act and regulations a final licence is required for diversion, use or storage of water for power purposes when such water is located on lands belonging to Her Majesty in right of Canada. Such a final licence is not granted until completion of the project. The normal sequence

Questions
of events is for the agency or company interested in developing a water power project which falls within the purview of these regulations to apply for a survey permit which permits the applicant to enter upon lands belonging to Her Majesty in right of Canada to survey and investigate the project for a period of up to three years. Survey permits are issued by the director of water power.
(b)	On completion of these preliminary surveys and investigations and subject to the conditions set forth in the regulations, the applicant may apply for a priority permit which shall give the applicant priority over other applicants in the consideration of his general layout plans if filed within the time specified in the permit. A priority permit is issued by the minister and is effective for a period of up to one year; it may be extended for a period of up to one year under certain conditions. Such permit shall in no case be construed as binding the minister to issue an interim licence nor as giving the applicant any exclusive claim or right.
(c)	The minister may issue to the applicant an interim licence for the carrying out of the proposed development when he is satisfied that the proposed development is the best possible in the public interest.
(d)	On completion of the project the minister may issue a final licence covering it for a term not exceeding 50 years from the date fixed in the original interim licence for the completion of the initial development.
(e)	On 6 July 1954 Northwest Power Industries Limited applied for a priority permit which was issued on 18 August 1954 by the minister, Hon. Jean Lesage.
(f)	On 22 July 1955 the company applied for an extension of this permit and such extension for a period of one year was issued by the acting minister, Hon. J. J. McCann.
(g)	On 20 August 1956 the company applied for a new priority permit on the grounds of the magnitude of the surveys and studies required on which it already had spent $812,000 and this second priority permit was issued on 28 August 1956 by the minister, Hon. Jean Lesage.
(h)	On 16 August the company applied for an extension to the second priority permit and a one year extension was granted on 28 August 1957 by the minister, Hon. Alvin Hamilton.
(i)	On 22 August 1958 the company applied for a third priority permit for the same reasons covering its application for the second priority permit and this third permit was issued on 11 November 1958 by the minister, Hon. Alvin Hamilton.

(j)	On 5 November 1959 the company applied for an extension to the third priority permit which was not granted as the company produced no evidence of having incurred additional expense on the survey and study under the third priority permit. However, a fourth priority permit was issued to the company on 6 January 1960 by the minister, Hon. Alvin Hamilton, with the advice that this fourth priority permit was the last that would be issued to the company or its associates for this project on the basis of the investigations and studies carried out by the company to that date.
2.	The conditions prescribed in the permit are those contained in the regulations.
3.	The names of the two ministers and one acting minister issuing the four permits and extensions are given in 1 above.
4.	As stated in 1 above, a priority permit can be issued only for a maximum of one year with an extension for a maximum of one year also.
5.	Permits and extensions expired-see answer to 4 above.
6.	The ministers concerned left office at various dates in accordance with constitutional practice.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the United States treasury informed us on Saturday that they were setting up an interdepartmental committee. They emphasized that the committee will be concerned with implementing the arrangement jointly announced on Sunday, July 21 under which a general blanket exemption from the proposed interest equalization tax is to be provided for new Canadian security issues. No limitation to or derogation from that agreement is involved. The new committee would not be involved in considering and approving particular Canadian security issues. Such activity would be incompatible with the general blanket exemption to be provided for new Canadian issues.
I think it is fair to say that we can welcome the proposed interdepartmental committee if it leads to a serious and continuing study of the Canada-United States balance of payments position by several United States departments and agencies concerned. Our case for the proposed blanket exemption, including outstanding securities as well as new issues, is very firmly based on the facts of the special, in fact I might say the unique, position of Canada-United States relationships. It is desirable that these facts should be understood as widely as possible in Washington and elsewhere.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Justice based on the replies I got from the Solicitor General last Thursday and Friday. Is the minister prepared to undertake an investigation to establish whether there is any substance to the allegations that the chartered banks are in fact circumventing and violating the statutory 6 per cent interest rate limit on loans?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FUEL OIL SUPPLY, NATIONAL DEFENCE ESTABLISHMENT, NICOLET, QUE.
subtopic: REPORTED VIOLATION OF INTEREST CEILING BY CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I am prepared to undertake an investigation, but surely the hon. member knows that there is a royal commission on banking which is sitting from one end of the country to the other, and surely representations of the kind he has brought to the attention of the house can be made to that commission. However, I did discuss the matter more particularly with the deputy minister of justice, and I

am informed by him that subsection 2 of section 93 of the Bank Act authorizes a bank to charge for the keeping of an account of a customer where the charge is made by an express agreement between the bank and the customer. Such a charge is usually made in connection with keeping an account established at the time a loan or advance is made by the bank. If the agreement with the customer for the keeping of the account is an "express agreement"-the quoted words are those used in subsection 2 of section 93- a bank is entitled to make the charge agreed to expressly with its customer notwithstanding that interest of up to 6 per cent may also be charged in respect of the loan or advance.

maintopic: FUEL OIL SUPPLY, NATIONAL DEFENCE ESTABLISHMENT, NICOLET, QUE.
subtopic: REPORTED VIOLATION OF INTEREST CEILING BY CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I realize that there is going to be a revision of the Bank Act and that there will be an opportunity for us to review its provisions, but the allegation that has been made is that violation of the present statute has been taking place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FUEL OIL SUPPLY, NATIONAL DEFENCE ESTABLISHMENT, NICOLET, QUE.
subtopic: REPORTED VIOLATION OF INTEREST CEILING BY CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext: I have seen the press statement to which my hon. friend refers, and if it is the same one which he has in mind what was said was "Strictly speaking it may be said that we are breaking the Bank Act". But when one looks at subsection 2 of section 93 there is unquestionably a right to make such a charge over and above the 6 per cent referred to in the act.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to answer a question asked in my absence by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso) on the exemption from visa requirements for non-immigrants coming to Canada as tourists.
I am happy to inform the hon. members that, as from September 15 of this year, the citizens of Italy, Greece, Portugal, Spain and Turkey will be able to enter Canada without a visa for visits of three months or less. Italy, Greece, Portugal, Spain and Turkey are, as well as Canada, members of the Organization for European Economic Cooperation. The Canadian government's decision is consistent with one of the general purposes of that organization, as it promotes easier travelling between citizens of member countries.

This decision represents another step forward in the Canadian long-term program tending to exempt from visas the non-immigrant tourists who are on a short visit in Canada. Experience has shown that this method is very convenient, as it simplifies the admission formalities.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution on the order paper which I have the honour to move, seconded by the hon. member for Laurier, involves perhaps the most difficult of all tasks which members of parliament have to discharge; because in dealing with
Senate and House of Commons Act this resolution they are, of course, dealing with their own personal interests. But I am confident, Mr. Chairman, that no member of parliament, no single member of parliament, whatever attitude he may take, will approach this task or come to a conclusion in regard to it in any selfish or self-centred way.
This resolution, Mr. Chairman, involves a responsibility which, if action is to be taken at all, cannot be escaped either by the government of the day or by parliament itself, since it cannot be delegated to any other body. If any decision is to be made in these matters covered by this resolution, that decision has to be made here. I indicated, Mr. Chairman, on Thursday last, and I quote from Hansard, page 2604:
Subject to further consultation between the house leader and hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to procedure, the government is ready to take the responsibility tomorrow of proposing certain changes in the remuneration and pensions of members of parliament,-
The government is not seeking to avoid its responsibility to recommend and I am quite happy, as it is indeed my duty as leader of the government and speaking on behalf of the government, to put this recommendation before the committee. We do not ask opposition parties to share the responsibility of making the recommendation; that is our responsibility. But we did inform representatives of all parties, representatives who were entitled to speak for those parties, as to what the government intended to propose, through the usual channels of communication between the house leader and representatives of parties opposite.
I am advised by the house leader that he received an assurance that none of the three parties opposite would oppose the measure which is being proposed in this resolution, and it is because of that fact, as well as for other reasons, that this resolution is being moved by me, the leader of the government. While it was indicated that there was not agreement to proceed on Friday last, the house leader did receive an assurance from all parties that there was agreement to proceed today, and that agreement is recorded in Hansard for Thursday last at page 2662, as follows:

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, PENSIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Then, on Monday, I am advised there is general agreement on all sides of the house that if the government will put on the order paper the motion regarding the remuneration and pensions of members of parliament there would be no objection raised to going ahead with all stages except third reading on Monday. The third reading would be held over until the next day.
He went on to say:
If that, correctly represents the sense of the house, and it can be so ordered, I will undertake that notice of the resolution will be given tomorrow

Senate and House of Commons Act
evening so that it will appear in Votes and Proceedings. That provides the 48 hours' notice required by the rules.
That has been done, Mr. Chairman, and it is on the basis of that decision of the house that the government is proceeding in this matter today.
If this resolution is accepted by the committee then there will be opportunity to deal with the details of the legislation subsequently, and I do not propose to go into these details this afternoon. Indeed, it would not be appropriate in discussing the resolution itself. The resolution is before the committee, and I think it is pretty clear in its terms.
As a result of our views the government has come to the conclusion to proceed to put the matter before parliament. It seems to the government that action on this matter is needed, and that it is needed now.
Perhaps I might be permitted to mention briefly some of the reasons why, in our view, such action is required. It is not primarily because of individual considerations. That is certainly an important consideration and none of us wish to escape from that consideration, but it is because the action we recommend will, in our view, increase the effectiveness of our parliamentary institutions.
In the first place there has been no revision of members' indemnities since 1954, almost ten years ago, despite very marked increases in remuneration in other fields o activity, and despite the fact that the increased cost of living during those 10 years has been recognized in so many fields of activity, and rightly so. Costs, as we all know, have gone up during those 10 years. Not only have the expenses of members as members, and the expenses of members as individuals, increased during that time, but the sessions of parliament have grown steadily longer. Although we hope shortly to set up a committee which will go into the whole question of parliamentary procedure and perhaps reshape our parliamentary institutions to make them more effective, nevertheless it does not seem to me that anything we do in this connection is likely to shorten the length of sessions of parliament in Ottawa to any considerable extent because of the increasing responsibilities of government and the increasing responsibilities of parliament. I myself cannot think that these responsibilities are likely to be diminished in the years ahead.
Therefore we have to face the fact that members of the House of Commons, to all intents and purposes, now have a full time occupation which is very different indeed from the situation which existed not so very many decades ago. This means that practically all members, except those fortunate enough to

live in Ottawa or very close to it, have to maintain two residences. There is all that this involves in terms of expense, as well as inconvenience, and indeed some sacrifice that has to be made to maintain two residences for the greater part of the year.
I think it is correct to say, Mr. Chairman, and I mention this with some hesitation because it does involve the personal affairs of members, but it has a bearing on this matter, that in order to discharge their responsibilities in parliament as members would wish to see them discharged, many members, especially new members who have come down here recently, find themselves in debt and they have made, and are making, many financial sacrifices which they should not be asked to make.
There is evidence on all sides, and a lot of it has been given to me in confidence- indeed I have been very much impressed and a little distressed by it-to support that statement that a great many members are making financial sacrifices which they should not be asked to make, quite apart from the additional sacrifices of disruption of family life, difficulties of education and that sort of domestic problem.
There is also a further consideration which perhaps it is appropriate for me to mention, and maybe those who have responsibilities in other parties will be able to confirm this- I know I certainly can confirm it from my own experience-that it is becoming increasingly difficult to attract or to secure candidates because of the direct financial loss involved, especially for young candidates and young members with young and growing families. There is this financial difficulty, and it is compounded by the difficulty of making provision for old age and other hazards.
Surely it is important to make sure that parliament does not lose its truly representative character because a financial barrier is added to other difficulties in devoting the time and energy which is required to public service. It seems to me if we do not discharge our responsibilities along the lines of this resolution at this time, we may soon find it will be impossible for some citizens in this country to make the financial sacrifices which they would like to be able to make, and which are involved in standing as a candidate for the House of Commons and acting as a member of the House of Commons. In that case, if it does reach that point, then the broadly representative character of the house will be changed, and we will find it becoming increasingly representative of those who can afford to make these sacrifices and those who perhaps are a little older, who

have retired from business and are in a position to accept the responsibilities and sacrifices involved.
It seems to me quite clear that no one is likely to become rich, or even to save money, out of the proposed remuneration if he or she discharges responsibilities to the people that he or she represents, as they should be discharged, and as members of the house do their best to discharge in present conditions. I think it will certainly be agreed there is a real need in these difficult days in our democratic and parliamentary institutions, when their effectiveness and representative character are questioned on so many sides, to attract men and women of ability to parliament and public life. I hope the resolution which I have the honour to move this afternoon will help in that regard and will make it possible for these men and women to accept and discharge the tremendous responsibilities placed upon members of parliament today.
Then, Mr. Chairman, there is the question of pension arrangements, which will be dealt with in the bill which will follow this resolution if the resolution is acceptable to the house. These pension provisions would be consequential upon the scale of remuneration, with one change, and I think it must surely be a change that will commend itself to us all, especially in the light of experience in the past. There will be provision made for widows of members of parliament. The lack of any such provision in the past has, I know, been a continuing source of anxiety to members for a good many years. Some of us have had personal experience of that anxiety and, indeed, of the suffering that can be caused and has been caused on one or two occasions in recent years by the fact that members' widows have been left almost destitute.
This resolution is in my name but the bill itself is in the name of the Secretary of State, who was delegated by the cabinet to work with officials in preparing the measure and who is available to the committee and the house to explain the details at the appropriate time.
Mr. Chairman, I recommend this resolution to the house. I think it would be false economy not to take action at this time which will enable members of parliament to discharge their increasingly onerous responsibilities without the financial worry that so many of them now have. In that way we will be making the House of Commons more effective, and in making the House of Commons more effective we will be making it possible for ourselves as members of the House of Commons to do more, and to do it more effectively for the people of Canada.

My own idea was that we would bring that in just before the election. But as it turned out, we did not have very much latitude in determining when that election would be held. I agree with the Prime Minister when he says there is a continual need to rejuvenate the house, to bring in new ideas, as young men and women do.
I do not intend to refer to any of the other provisions because at the moment they are still in general form. I will mention one, however, which has to do with former prime ministers. I do not expect this is going to apply to me, because I have other hopes. The fact that it is to apply to prime ministers who have held their position for four years seems to indicate that the present Prime Minister believes that with the support of other parts of the house he will be in office for that length of time.
I am interested in this proposal for the payment of leaders of parties other than the official parties. Both of those hon. gentlemen are estimable. Both of them are a credit to the House of Commons. But I would point out one fact: Under our parliamentary system this would indeed be a divergence from the whole concept of parliamentary government in the British tradition. Our system recognizes only the government and the opposition party which has the largest number of members. It is interesting to go back and find out how the opposition came by its name, and it is very pertinent today. The title "Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition" goes back to the year 1826, when Mr. Hobhouse, one of the greatest parliamentarians of his time, afterwards Lord Broughton, while engaging in an attack on Mr. Canning used these words:

Senate and House of Commons Act
It is said to be hard on His Majesty's ministers to raise objections of this character but it is more hard on His Majesty's opposition to compel them to take this course.
Canning referred to the use of this expression and stated in his reply:
My right honourable friend could not have invented a better phrase to designate us than that which he adopted. That we are certainly to all intents and purposes a branch of His Majesty's government its proceedings for some time past have proven. Although with the gentlemen opposite in office, we are in power, the measures are ours but the emoluments are theirs.
That was in 1826, and that has been the designation since. If a means can be reached whereby these two gentlemen could be helped to provide those services which are necessary for them I would say nothing to the contrary. But if, as a result of this action, the entire background of our British parliamentary development which contemplates a government that governs and an opposition, composed of the largest group, which opposes, were to be set aside, then I merely point out that the government may well be introducing a multiplication and proliferation of parties in the years ahead and that our system does not work as effectively as it would if we had two-party government.
I say this with the greatest respect to those in third parties because I know very well that, had there not been a third party in the 'twenties the old age pensions legislation would never have gone through. But Mr. King needed two or three votes and Mr. Woods-worth and Mr. Heaps provided those votes in return for action. When I make this statement I am not in any way being critical of them or of their ability and capacity. I am simply pointing out that this will be a step toward a multiplication of parties within our political system. It is a step which some may feel would be a worthy one. My reading of history and my experience do not place me among those who are its proponents. I realize too that if this legislation were delayed until after the next election, I guess we would not get it through at all because there are members in some of the parties who would not feel constrained to support the government until such time as another election took place.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has stated that this is a responsibility we cannot put off on others. The provision as to ex-prime ministers is one that causes me concern, whatever the future may bring, in that by casting my vote for it I would actually be placing myself in the position of voting for my own benefit, provided I were to qualify, as I hope I never do. That is the position with many members of the house.

I remember the last speech that Mr. King made in parliament in which he endeavoured to give parliament the benefit of his years in public life. He spoke of the overwhelming need to assure that the closing of the door of parliament should not mean the opening of the door to the poorhouse for those in public life. I think it was one of the most impressive and emotional speeches that he ever made. He was describing Laurier house and the terrible difficulty he had in financing it. He said in part:
There is an impression among a great many people in this country that Laurier house has been maintained by the state. It has been maintained by myself personally out of my own pocket and my own income, and if I have not been able to invite my hon. friend and some members who are about me at the moment and many others as often as I should like to have done and extended as much in the way of hospitality as I should like to have done, that is one of the reasons.
I remember that speech in which he told parliament of all the financial difficulties that are incident to high position in the state. As a matter of fact, I surmise that out of that came the establishment of 24 Sussex street as the official home of the Prime Minister.

I am also fully aware of the very serious problems faced by a number of members, many young members. It is because of that I believe some action should be taken. However, there are certain portions of the resolution which, when translated into bill form and made clear thereby, will need careful consideration and examination at that time.
I want to say to all members in all parts of the house that the manner in which they received the introductory words of the Prime Minister showed a reserve and self-control that was most admirable. I am not going to say more at this time. I have simply stated that this is a matter for the conscience of each member, to be determined by him in accordance with his conscientious views and desires to insure that this institution will always be a palladium of freedom. It is my intention to speak directly and briefly to the principle and basic intent of this resolution. I will in no way attempt to enter into political debate. In our

Senate and House of Commons Act opinion, the time has come, if not already overdue, when the remuneration of members of the House of Commons should be increased. It is well known the present cost of living, and the essential expenses of members of parliament, are in most cases more than they receive. An increase is necessary, first of all to enable members of parliament to pay their way. It is essential also in order to attract and to hold the type of people that Canadians need as their representatives in this House of Commons.
I believe it would be wrong to make politics in Canada a money-making proposition and to eliminate entirely the public service motive. On the other hand, if members of parliament are not paid proportionately to their worth and their expected duties and expenses, this chamber will become a collecting point for the well-to-do, for those who have private means. It will not any longer be a representative assembly of the people. While we have not been informed beforehand of all of the details of the legislation which this resolution will introduce, the Social Credit members in caucus have decided that they are in favour of the principle of this measure. After considerable discussion our house leader and our party whip have so informed the government of the discussions which were conducted. As a party, we are prepared to shoulder our share of the political responsibility for this decision. The decision of our party in caucus was not made with complete unanimity, but the decision to which we have come is, I believe, the right one.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the Social Credit party I lend my support to this resolution.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, PENSIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The members of our party in caucus meeting, after a very thorough discussion and apparently unlike the members of the other two opposition parties, aware of the details as they were forwarded to us through the courtesy of the house leader, have approved this proposal of the government to improve the salaries, expense allowance and pensions of members of parliament and other features of the resolution as indicated, including a pension for former prime ministers. I have difficulty, Mr. Chairman, restraining myself at this time from making remarks of sheer, bitter anger after listening to the Leader of the Opposition. It somehow seemed to me he wanted to draw into this discussion the definition of politics as the conduct of public affairs for private advantage.
I do not see this resolution, the purposes that it intends, and the members of all parties in this parliament as being in a position to need that kind of line drawn for them today. I know it may be presumptuous of me to say that, but I could review all the


discussions regarding salary increments over the last three or four years, and I can inform the committee that I had some part in them, as an interlocutor at least, because I first introduced the matter as a private members' grievance about four years ago.
As a consequence I was supported-and I have the letters to show it-by members of all parties, including a great many members of the party represented by the Leader of the Opposition. I happen to know that several times in the ensuing years there were tentative negotiations carried on by private members supporting the government, to try and get something done on this matter. They were always full of optimism but they were not getting anywhere.
When I think of the turnover we have had in membership of the house in the last few elections I realize why so many of these people came and went. Many of them were supporters of the Leader of the Opposition but now they have departed, and many of them departed very bitter over the fact that nothing was done and that there was no co-ordinated or co-operative approach on the part of all parties to do something about members' indemnities.
In the four elections we have had in the past five years there has been a tremendous turnover in membership of the House of Commons. When I got up and spoke in the house in favour of more money for members of parliament, and repeated that several years later in the form of a resolution, I did not get much in the way of obvious support. However I think most hon. members came along to me later and said it was a great idea, but they thought I was a knucklehead and that I was throwing away an opportunity for re-election.
In this connection I would like to point out to those hon. members, who may be apprehensive of the fact that some people will tell them that what we are doing is an unprincipled thing, that in two election campaigns my actions were used against me and I did not have much trouble surviving them. I am not saying this is a pattern for all hon. members of the house, but I want to make it clear that this tremendous fear, that especially seems to be built up amongst older members of the house, that this is a terrible thing with which to face our electors, is much overdrawn and exaggerated.
I think the people of the country to whom we are looking for an interest and support in politics will understand and appreciate that this is not only something to improve the calibre of the House of Commons but it is something which has been necessary for a long, long time.

One of the most apparent consequences after listening to the Leader of the Opposition is to ask the question, why did he not introduce the select committee? Why did he not do something about a select committee to have an open discussion about salaries of members of parliament? I am sure the situation was almost as serious a little over a year ago when my resolution was before the house; but the word went out that there was to be no discussion on it, and after one limp little speech by the mover of the resolution, that was it.
It seems to me that in this, as in so many other matters, you cannot have it both ways in the house. You cannot play it along both lines. Either you are for or against something like this, and I know the majority of the members are not only behind the resolution but behind the measure in general as the details have come out; and this will be proved if it is put to a vote.
One of the things that follows from what I think will be generous and sizeable increases in our emoluments, which will enable us to do a better job, is that we will have to meet a higher standard. I know from my own sizing up of the situation in my constituency, and from talking to members of other parties, that the increments that will be available if this measure is passed will induce a great many people into running for the candidacies for all parties. This will be good. In other words, instead of improving our own chances, in many ways we are hurting them.
If that argument is worth anything, then I think we need to acknowledge we are not the most brilliant assemblage in the world. We know the House of Commons could be much more representative of Canada, and I think most of us will agree that this measure will do something about bringing people with wider backgrounds, wider experience and more knowledge into the political field. So far as we are concerned, that will be all to the good.
The attitude may develop out of the discussion which takes place today that for some months we must face a raging debate, back and forth across the country, on whether members of parliament have been shameful in supporting and putting through such a measure as this. I do not believe for a minute that such a debate will continue if each of us has the courage, as individual members, to go out and face our constituents and let them know why this is done. I appeal as an individual member-not as a member of my own party-to all members of all parties to do this, because I am afraid that it may get to be nasty and difficult if the pattern that
Senate and House of Commons Act was set by the contribution of the Leader of the Opposition should be carried any further.
We in this party support the intention of the resolution. So far as we know them we support the details, although we might have had some quarrel about some of the levels if we had received more consultation. However, we do not propose to put up a great many speakers on the motion. We are all for it, and I think future parliamentarians of the country will be grateful to us for supporting it.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Pickersgill thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-91, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act and the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with two minutes to look at a bill containing 14 clauses I am not very well informed as to its details; that is, shall I say, its minor details and those provisions which are particularly related to the pension aspects of the bill. I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the previous speakers and I have given a great deal of thought to this difficult, decuple and delicate question during recent months. As one who has a Victorian appreciation of the value of money, the virtues of simple living and who suffers the pinpricks of a combined Anglican and socialist conscience, I have made several agonizing reappraisals of the situation in recent months. I am speaking now to express my point of view and to be as fair as possible. I wish to give a brief review of the history of sessional indemnities. It has been mentioned in some respects previously, but I have been asked to do this by persons outside the house.
In the first instance I understand that members of parliament received about $600 per annum as a sessional indemnity; later this was raised to $1,000 and then $4,000 for a number of years. Then on December 13, 1945

Senate and House of Commons Act -I remember the day well, Mr. Speaker-the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King made a motion to provide an allowance of $2,000 for incidental expenses in addition to the $4,000 indemnity. Mr. Maclnnis, the then hon. member for Vancouver East, and the member for Kootenay West were, if I remember correctly, the only two who spoke against and voted against this increase. It was a most interesting debate. The prime minister in reply disagreed strongly with our arguments and later ticked me off when replying to what I had said on that occasion. I want to bring to the attention of the house the fact that prior to introducing that resolution the prime minister of the day informed the Canadian people, during the election campaign, of his intention to provide for an expense allowance.
The next increase came as the result of a resolution, introduced by the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent on January 26, 1954, of which the prime minister of that day had given the electors notice in a radio broadcast in which he said something to the effect that he was going to make the responsibilities of members less burdensome. At this time the sessional indemnity was increased from $4,000 to $8,000, thus making a total of $10,000. The then hon. member for Vancouver East, Mr. Maclnnis, opposed the increase and voted against it.
Then we have had the recent efforts of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who on April 28, 1959 urged an increase of the sessional indemnity to $12,000 and an expense allowance of $3,000. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I give him credit for his courage in bringing forward what was considered to be a very delicate and risky question under those circumstances. He was supported by the then hon. member for Winnipeg North.
I think that was the end of the support. Then on December 19, 1960 the hon. member for Port Arthur asked a question of the prime minister as to whether a parliamentary pay raise would have to be a package deal which would include a daily roll call. On March 19, 1962 he moved a simple resolution and proposed an increase of the sessional indemnity to $10,000 and an expense allowance of $3,000. He mentioned at that time that this increase would be sufficient to meet his particular needs and problems.
On January 28, 1963 the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) asked the minister of justice to protect certain members of his group against certain acts of violence that might occur as suggested by a very famous newspaper columnist if there were any attempt to oppose an increase in sessional indemnities. Numerous editorials have been written across Canada on this question, both


for and against. I have seen two such editorials recently, one representing the Conservative view, and entitled "A Conservative view", by Mr. Frank McGee, in the Daily Star of July 27, 1963, and the other by the hon. member for Port Arthur entitled "Now we'll have to earn our pay"-I agree with him on that point-in the Telegram of July 27, 1963.
There are arguments for and against on this question. The arguments in favour of an increase have generally been, I think, that first it makes it possible for any person with limited means to be elected to parliament. I think that is a reasonable and sound argument. A second argument is that it makes it attractive to the well-to-do, almost a bait to the well-to-do, to run for parliament. I do not think that is a sound argument because throughout the years we have had a good number of well-to-do persons who have represented Canadians in this house without, I am quite sure, any regard to the sessional indemnity and things of that sort. A third argument is that it is necessary to ensure the independence of members. I think that is right; I think it is very necessary that members of parliament should receive an indemnity and an allowance that remove any possibility of temptation for a weak man.
Then again, Mr. Speaker, the argument in recent years has been that a great many members in this house actually need an increase in order to meet their living expenses and other costs. I agree with that argument and I think that is generally accepted. I realize myself, although I am one who has given a great deal of thought to this question, it is a difficult thing for members to decide. I have been most reluctant psychologically, you might say, to come to certain conclusions. I know this is a sound reason for increasing the indemnity. Fortunately money is not always attractive either to the rich or poor. Our history is replete with the names of first-class people both rich and poor who have served this country in parliament since confederation. I refer to such men as Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and then the late J. S. Woodsworth, who I remember made a great sacrifice to serve the Canadian people. I have known of him travelling on day coaches day after day, rather than take a sleeper in order to save that additional expense to the C.C.F. club paying his expenses. There have been numerous people willing to make some sacrifice in connection with representing the public. I remember the efforts made by the late John MacNicol with respect to the question of the conservation of Canadian resources. I think he was a man of some substance who between sessions

travelled through western Canada lecturing and doing whatever he could, far beyond the bounds of duty, because of his particular interest in this question.
The arguments against an increase, Mr. Speaker, are usually two, from what I have read and heard. First of all, the members entered into a contract with their electors during the last election to serve on the basis on the present indemnity and allowance. Some newspapers have supported this point of view. Some radio talks have supported the same point of view. Second, on moral grounds, therefore, any increase should only become effective after the next election. I believe an increase is a problem which has been dodged by members for two or three years and should have been dealt with before this.
Now a few words with respect to this bill. I have not read it, although I know the main substance of it. I usually like an opportunity to read a bill carefully before speaking on it in the house, but I trust that as we go through the committee stage we will have the opportunity to ask questions and to find out what we see through a glass darkly at this time.
First of all, let me say that I think it was unfortunate that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the leader of the Conservative party did not during the election campaign do as the former Right Hon. Mackenzie King did and as the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent did, and announce to the Canadian people during the campaign that they believed that members of parliament should have an increase in their indemnities and expense accounts. I think in that respect they failed to inform the people. I am firmly convinced that many members of this house cannot make ends meet on the present indemnity and allowance. I know as a result of discussions that various members, especially the younger members with families who are required to establish two residences and move their children backwards and forwards sometimes between their constituencies and Ottawa, have incurred very serious and in some cases quite large obligations. In fact, I was almost shocked to hear of the way a few members have got into debt as a result of becoming members of parliament and performing their functions as such. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that there will be quite a number of bank managers in Canada who will give a sigh of relief when this legislation has been adopted by this house.

After careful consideration of the question I have come to the conclusion that a total
Senate and House of Commons Act of $15,000 would be an adequate raise; that is to say, $10,000 indemnity and $5,000 expense allowance. I think there are members of all parties who thought that they would be fortunate even to get that amount. I am one who feels that there should always be an element of sacrifice on the part of those who enter any level of public life; otherwise being a member of parliament or a member of the legislature simply becomes a profession and the spirit and the willingness to serve is lost. I believe there is still a place for honour in this dollar-hungry materialistic world, an honour that prompts thousands of Canadians to serve without any thought of remuneration on school boards, hospital boards, irrigation district boards and in many other community organizations. It is very fortunate for us that we have these people who regard it as an honour, a privilege and a duty to serve their districts and their communities.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, and I am speaking frankly, this is a very generous increase, more than was expected, as I have said before, by some members of all parties of the house. In my opinion, to justify it we will have to do certain things. First of all, I think we will have to recognize from this point on that being a member of parliament is a full time vocation that presents a particular challenge under the circumstances of today. Second, Mr. Speaker, I believe that it should provide for an attendance regulation which will end the Thursday to Tuesday club, and I hope that the regulations are such that this will result. Third, this increase should make it possible for all members to employ a secretary in their riding during any recess of parliament. Members often require a secretary. Those of us who live in country ridings often have to travel for a week or so at a time, returning home without a secretary, having to pound away at the typewriter for several days, which has been my experience, and then leave on another trip without any opportunity for leisure, recreation and so on. Fourth, I think this generous increase will make it possible for all members of parliament to meet the normal and usual requests for donations to good causes without any financial discomfort. It provides a greater opportunity in that respect. Fifth, it does provide a glorious opportunity for those who do not require more than $15,000 to use the balance in support of worth-while community enterprises. I am sure there are some hon. members of the house quite willing to carry on with what is required here and to use any surplus they have to the advantage of the communities in which they live.

Sixth, I am very glad, Mr. Speaker, that the legislation will provide for a survivors' pension plan. I am sure we all have personal knowledge of widows of members of parliament being left in very difficult and unfortunate circumstances. I am pleased that a pension plan is being placed on a sound actuarial basis and that the means test on members' pensions is being removed. You know, Mr. Speaker, there are only two categories of persons under pension in Canada who are subject to a means test. The first are members of parliament, and the second the recipients of war veterans allowance. I hope and trust the removal of this means test from members' pensions points to a similar consideration being given to the recipients of war veterans allowance; and I see the Prime Minister is taking a great interest in what I have to say on this point.
Regardless of any difference of opinion as to the amount required to meet members' costs, living expenses and allowances, this increase can only be justified, in our opinion, if first we stand up for Canada as a free and independent nation with the right to develop its own foreign and defence policies. We are not a great military power but we can be a great moral force by giving leadership to all those nations who look to us for that leadership in the promotion of world peace through the strengthening of international organizations and responsibilities. Second, we must make certain that parliament provides every Canadian with a standard of living and the basic security to which a free industrious and independent people living in a land of plenty are entitled. Third, we must make certain to conserve our natural resources to the advantage of this and future generations of Canadians, including the surplus waters of the Columbia and the Kootenay rivers, which will be required by the Canadians who live in the Okanagan valley and on the prairies in the years ahead.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say simply this: If we fail to do this, then by accepting this increase we shall be guilty of accepting money under false pretenses.

Never yet having been defeated I had not had occasion until recently, to find out whether the new member or the old member was paid for election day, but I was advised by the officials when I was helping to prepare this bill that the defeated member does not get paid for election day; it is the successful one who does.

The total would now be $120 for each such day and I am sure we all agree that taking into account such a generous allowance, namely 21 days absence during which no deduction is suffered, this is a proper figure.
I would like to endorse what the hon. member for Red Deer has said, namely that with the kind of remuneration we will now receive we should take more seriously than we have sometimes, perhaps, in the past, our responsibility to be here. I agree that this is not the kind of thing to put in a bill but I would offer two suggestions. First we might consider this matter in the special committee on procedure, whenever that is established. The other suggestion is that perhaps this is a matter for discipline within each of our party organizations. Senate and House of Commons Act and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and I will fight them on it in the rules committee if it is ever set up.
I have heard it said often in the past that members must answer a roll call in the House of Commons to let everyone know that they are in attendance. I have spent a great deal of my life under discipline of one sort or another, whether in school or in the army, and I react strongly against suggestions that there should be this type of discipline for members of parliament. This is an institution unique in this country and if members do not have a sense of responsibility, their constituents will soon discover it and they will retire them, as has happened to so many people who were in this chamber.
