Mr. Chairman, with the remuneration we previously received I was quite happy in seeking election on a number of occasions to declare my attendance in the house and I have always been happy to do so. I know there are those in the house who know much more about legislation than I do, and who will say that you cannot write these things into a bill. Maybe we should not have put any amount of money in the bill either. Maybe we should have left these things up in the air. Then if the accountant found that the money in the treasury was sufficient to give us a certain amount that could then be done. However, it has not been thought

right to do that and I do not think there are many members who would support a proposition of that kind.
I do think we have an obligation to the country at least to provide a record of attendance in the house although I admit at times members may be somewhere else for legitimate reasons. There are members who have said over the years that they have had to supplement their incomes elsewhere, and I think this may have been true. It is quite true that some have a higher standard of living than others and if you become accustomed to a certain standard of living it is not very pleasant to have to reduce it. Being a member of parliament certainly has meant a reduction in the standard of living of many people, even a reduction in my standard of living as a trade union representative, because I believe my take-home pay here is less than what I received in that job. If this is true in my case, I am sure there are many professions where the difference is greater. Therefore someone would say, perhaps legitimately, that he could not be here on Monday because he had to be in his office and he might also say that he could not be here on Tuesday, Thursday and Friday because he had to be in his office.
There may be some justification for that; but if we pass a bill of this type providing fair and reasonable remuneration, then we also have an obligation to the country to show that there is some method of recording attendance. I have heard the former prime minister, the member for Prince Albert, say on several occasions that there should be no restrictions placed on a member so long as he could say that he was working in the interests of his constituents, and that he could be doing so either in Ottawa or in his riding. With that I agree, but this is where I think a problem will arise.
I was given the opportunity of addressing a meeting the other day that involved many of the representatives of the municipalities in my riding. The problem concerned me and I was asked to discuss these matters with them. I would think I did so in my capacity as their representative in parliament. It is probably true that I was in my riding when certain bills were being dealt with here that I should have been present to discuss, but I think there are times when matters are being dealt with in your riding that are as much your responsibility as your duties in the House of Commons. I think that is where the dilemma will arise.
It is difficult for me to decide whether he should be at a fall fair or at the opening of a bridge or in the House of Commons. I think this is where the member's own responsibility and integrity will come into the
29, 1963
Senate and House of Commons Act picture, when he makes a decision as to where he is going to be. In my view there can be no objection to a roll call. I have been associated with many organizations where there was a roll call of the officers at every meeting. Every officer was not always present, but quite often someone would rise and say that brother so and so is not here because he is at work or attending to something else. Honest, legitimate reasons were given for his not being there. I do not know how we can arrive at that in the House of Commons. If the 21 days are tied to the roll call it may be that that would be unfair. We are very stupid in devising solutions for something that does not appear to be obviously easy, and so we may have difficulty in arriving at a solution in this regard.
But, Mr. Chairman, I think we have an obligation to the country and to parliament itself to ensure that attendance in the house is maintained. It really is no joke when you hear the expression "T to T boys". I think it is a disgrace to parliament and it has only been justified by the fact that many members were unable to carry out their responsibilities with the remuneration they received.
In making their recommendation I believe that the government has considered the job of a member of parliament to be a full time one, and therefore the representatives of the people should be prepared to give at least the major part of their time to the duties that have fallen upon them as a result of being elected to parliament. I believe that we must arrive at a much better method than this one of signing an affidavit. I am sure some members know of other members who have been signing these affidavits under what would be considered elsewhere to be dubious circumstances.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that this matter will be given consideration. I would particularly urge that the minister piloting this legislation try to insert something in clause 2 that would strengthen the interpretation of public and official business. I feel that each member will represent his constituency in a different manner from that of his fellow members even in the same party. I hope it will not be left to the whips themselves to police this provision because that will cause a great deal of dissension. I do think that they will strengthen public support for the institution of parliament, and support that will be necessary to those members participating in this debate if they wish to return to this house, if we give the public assurance that we have provided the necessary safeguards to ensure active attendance in this place.

I should like to say a word about this public service provision. Those who live a long distance from Ottawa cannot get home to a fall fair within a day, whereas those who live close to Ottawa can take a half day off, spend part of the time in parliament and still attend the fair. Those of us who live in the area of West Middlesex must be absent a whole day to attend a fall fair, unless we fly both ways.

I know the people in most of these constituencies do like to see their member come into the constituency to attend these functions. They invite the member to do that. If we are going to limit this provision to 21 days, I know from my own experience that 21 days will not begin to cover the events to which a member in that area is invited. I think it is much better to leave the interpretation of those words "public business" to the member. I know when I am conducting public business or when I am acting in my own interests. Mr. Chairman, I feel that an interesting suggestion could be made to the government on that point. It has often been said that we discuss legislation in this house but that we have not enough contacts with our constituents. Does the Secretary of State not think that it would be advisable to provide members with airplane passes between Ottawa and their ridings so that they could keep in closer touch with their electors?
For instance, Mr. Chairman, when I visit my constituency, which is situated in the Saguenay-Lake St. John district, I must leave the capital on Friday afternoon at ten minutes to five and I get home only the next morning at nine o'clock, after having spent a rather uncomfortable night because the railway is in a pitiful condition in that area. So, on Saturday, I have to spend the whole day at my office and then get ready to come back at a time which is not too convenient. Travelling in such a way, I am only able to sleep at home one night out of three. So if members who live some distance from Ottawa had the privilege of free travel aboard planes, it would be possible for them to leave Friday evening at six o'clock and to get to their constituency that same night. They could then sleep at least two nights at home and they would have two full days to devote to their electors.
As for me, at the present time, I am in contact with my electors only every fortnight, and that after having spent two nights on the train and not to mention the work I have to do right here. You will understand that such a schedule is rather tough, especially with sessions as long as they are now.

of Canada who desire judicial appointment is greater than they can reasonably be expected to make. The increases that will be proposed will be fair and more realistic than the present salary scale and will, I am confident, enable us to continue to have in Canada a judicial service of the highest integrity and quality.

of judges someone overlooked amending the pension statute. Although the judges, in this case the county court judges, received a salary increase from $8,000 to $10,000, the pension remained payable and is still payable on the basis of the original statute.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the hon. members who sit on this side of the house, I would feel remiss were I to let this opportunity go by without congratulating the Minister of Justice for this bill concerning the salary of judges in the different courts.
Due to the late hour, I will have only a few words to say on this bill which not only provides for a well deserved salary increase for the judges in the various courts, but deals also with the appointment of eight new judges to the superior court to fill a very great need. As you know, this is a civil law court in the province of Quebec. I also congratulate the minister for acting with such speed.
I remember that for many long years members of the bar, with the support of the newspapers, the trade unions and a host of public authorities, have been requesting the appointment of additional judges to the superior court. However, it was only in the last few weeks that the premier of Quebec, Mr. Jean Lesage, realized the situation and authorized the appointment of eight new judges in the districts mentioned by the Minister of Justice, particularly the district of St. Frangois-Bed-ford. I am sure that the appointment of a judge in the St. Frangois-Bedford district will greatly speed the administration of justice.
I take this opportunity for congratulating the Minister of Justice who, in such a short time, has done all he could to help the administration of justice. This is characteristic of the dynamic spirit of the federal government.
In addition, I hope the Minister of Justice will appoint those judges to the superior court before the fall sittings, which will make for a better administration of justice at the very beginning of the court hearings in September.
Since I do not want to delay the passage of this bill, I conclude my remarks by offering, on behalf of the lawyers from the province of Quebec and the hon members sitting on this side of the house, my congratulations to the Minister of Justice for this timely legislation.
